moments.title: The Anglo-Saxons arrive
moments.who: Angles, Saxons and Jutes from northern Germany and Denmark
moments.body: After Roman withdrawal from Britain (410 CE), Germanic settlers cross the North Sea. They bring related West Germanic dialects that, over centuries, fuse into Old English. The Celtic Britons retreat westward (Wales, Cornwall) or are absorbed.
moments.takeaway: English starts as a continental Germanic language imposed on a Celtic-then-Latin-then-Celtic substrate. The four main Old English dialects (West Saxon, Mercian, Northumbrian, Kentish) reflect the settlers' kingdoms.

moments.title: Old English literary culture
moments.who: Anonymous scops, Bede, Alfred the Great
moments.body: Beowulf (manuscript dated c. 1000, composition probably earlier) is the longest surviving Old English poem. Bede's Ecclesiastical History (731) is written in Latin but transmits Anglo-Saxon culture. Alfred (r. 871-899) sponsors translation of key Latin works into English and founds an English literary tradition.

quote.text: Hwæt! We Gar-Dena in geardagum / þeodcyninga þrym gefrunon.

moments.takeaway: Old English looks foreign to modern eyes — heavy with case endings, gendered nouns, a vocabulary 95% Germanic. The 'English' you speak today shares much less than half its vocabulary with this.

now.title: Anglo-Saxon survivals
now.body: The 100 most common words in modern English are overwhelmingly Anglo-Saxon: the, of, and, to, in, is, you, that, it, he, was, for. The 'core' vocabulary of family, body, weather, basic verbs (eat, sleep, walk, run, live, die) remains Germanic. Latin and French give the layered, formal vocabulary on top.
now.open_questions: How much of pre-Conquest English do we really know? The textual record is small and skewed (mostly religious, mostly West Saxon). Spoken varieties may have been very different.

items.reflection: Modern English keeps Old English bones inside a French-and-Latin skin. The difference between 'come' and 'arrive', 'kingly' and 'royal', 'house' and 'mansion' is a thousand-year-old social register.

moments.title: The Norman Conquest
moments.body: William defeats Harold at Hastings on 14 October. The English aristocracy is replaced by Norman French speakers. For roughly 300 years, England is trilingual: French for the court and aristocracy, Latin for the church and law, English for the common people.
moments.takeaway: 1066 doesn't kill English — it ranks it. English becomes the language of the conquered.

moments.title: Middle English absorbs French wholesale
moments.body: English borrows around 10,000 French words during this period — government (parliament, justice, court, prison), cuisine (beef, pork, mutton — vs. cow, pig, sheep for the live animals tended by English-speaking peasants), and abstract vocabulary. English also sheds most case endings and complicated gender — possibly accelerated by contact with Norse and French.
moments.takeaway: The Walter Scott observation (Ivanhoe, 1819) about animal/meat names is a real and revealing pattern.

moments.title: Statute of Pleading
moments.body: English is restored as the language of the law courts. Parliament is opened in English in 1362. Chaucer writes The Canterbury Tales (begun c. 1387) in English — and the choice itself is a political statement.
moments.takeaway: English's recovery is incomplete and slow. Latin and French persist in law and church well past 1500.

now.title: A hybrid language
now.body: Modern English vocabulary is roughly 26% Germanic, 29% French, 29% Latin, 6% Greek, and the rest borrowed from everywhere. We have layered synonyms (ask/question/interrogate, kingly/royal/regal) that map onto register. English's openness to loanwords — without an academy to police them — is a Norman inheritance.
now.open_questions: Was Middle English creolised? Some linguists (Bailey and Maroldt, 1977) argued English was a Norse/French/English creole; the mainstream view treats it as heavy contact-induced simplification but not full creolisation.

items.reflection: If you complain about French loanwords in English, you're complaining about a thousand years of English. The hybrid is the language.

moments.title: Caxton sets up shop at Westminster
moments.body: Caxton, who had learned printing in Cologne and Bruges, sets up England's first printing press at Westminster. He prints around 100 books, mostly in English — Chaucer, Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, his own translations. He faces a dialectal decision: which English to use?

quote.text: Loo, what sholde a man in thyse days now wryte, egges or eyren?

moments.takeaway: Caxton tells a story of merchants who couldn't get eggs because the locals didn't recognise the word. He chose East Midlands English (the dialect of London and the university towns) — the basis of modern Standard English.

moments.title: King James Bible
moments.body: The KJV becomes the most influential book in English. Its rhythms, its archaisms (already slightly old-fashioned in 1611), its absorption into common speech — 'the salt of the earth', 'a thorn in the flesh', 'the writing on the wall', 'the powers that be' — shape literary English for four centuries.
moments.takeaway: Together with Shakespeare's First Folio (1623), the KJV gives early modern English a prestigious standard.

moments.title: Johnson's Dictionary
moments.body: Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language' — 42,773 entries, written largely by Johnson alone over nine years — is the most influential dictionary before the OED. It uses illustrative quotations from literature, sets a tone of judicious authority, and helped fix spelling and meaning for the next century.
moments.takeaway: Johnson initially intended to 'fix' the language but came to accept that change was inevitable. The Preface is one of the great essays on lexicography.

now.title: Standard English now
now.body: Standard British English (sometimes 'BBC English' or 'received standard') is a written norm with broad consensus and a much looser spoken norm. American English diverged enough by the 19th century — Webster's 1828 dictionary deliberately reforms spelling (color, theater) and codifies an American standard. Global Englishes (Indian, Nigerian, Singaporean) are now spoken by more people than British and American combined.
now.open_questions: Will English fragment into mutually unintelligible varieties as Latin did into the Romance languages? Probably not, given continuous global media contact — but the question is taken seriously by linguists like David Crystal.

items.reflection: Standard English wasn't decreed; it was selected — by a printer's economic choice, a king's commission, a lexicographer's stamina, and a market of readers.
